TROOP NEWS 

Ewell McCants, a long-time Scouter, died 
last month, and Troop 1 14 provided an Honor 
Guard at his Rosary. Scouts Michael Erdman 
and Bob Williams were the Honor Guard, and 
they were lauded for the dignity with which 
they performed their duty. Scout Master George 
Williams and Cub Master Bob Lando also 
attended to represent all Scouts from our area, 
past and present. 

Several members of the Troop participated 
in a hike to the REACT Station atop San Bruno 
Mountain in November. Scout Master George 
Williams reported that there were a few sore mus- 
cles and joints after it was over, all of them his. 

PACK NEWS 

Pack 1 14 was at the top of the list in sales 
of tickets to the Family Fun Fair held at Fort 
Mason last month. In addition, their booth, the 
theme of which was "Cub Scout Fun," was well 
attended by patrons of the fair. 

The annual Pack Christmas Party will be 
held at the Pack meeting on Thursday, 
December 21st at the Glen Park Recreation 
Center. It will start at 7:30 p.m. # 


Neither rain nor sleet nor Monday Night 
Football could keep 47 hardy souls from 
coming to hear Speaker of the Assembly Leo 
McCarthy at the November GPA meeting. 
McCarthy represents the 18th Assembly 
District, which includes the southwest third of 
the City. Glen Park residents asked probing 
questions, and seemed impressed by his 
straightforward style. When the Assembly 
reconvened this month, McCarthy was unan- 
imously reelected Speaker by his colleagues.

Parking a Lot 


by Laura Goderez 

Two years ago, people in over 250 house- 
holds in the area directly adjacent to the Glen 
Park BART station signed a petition requesting 
Preferential Parking. This was a community 
effort to reclaim the streets from commuters 
who used all available parking, preventing resi- 
dents from parking near their own homes, 
blocking driveways, and reducing parking for 
merchants' customers. The bureaucratic wheels 
moved slowly, and so it is that the system has 
only just been installed. 

The Preferential Parking system has been 
used in many cities around the country and in 
other parts of San Francisco. It works by 
restricting parking for nonresidents while 
exempting residents from the restrictions by 
means of a sticker displayed on the residents car. 
Residents may then park in the restricted area 
without being ticketed, while long-term non- 
residential parkers will be fined for parking too 
long in restricted areas. Residents who use off- 
street parking (garages) need not purchase a 
sticker. 

Publicity about Preferential Parking in 
North Beach may be discouraging until one 
realizes that North Beach and Glen Park have 
very different parking problems. North Beach 
is largely commercial during the day and has an 
active night life as well, requiring extended 
hours of restriction (until 9:00 p.m.). There 
are many multiple dwelling units and consider- 
able resident turn-over, all resulting in confusion 
over who is and who is not entitled to purchase 
a Sticker. (Continued on page 1 7)

St. Anthony's, Thanksgiving Day 


by James Godfrey 

James Godfrey 's writing has appeared in a variety of publications including Pacific Sun, New 
Voices, and The English Record. He teaches classes in creative writing through U.C. Extension, and 
has originated two teaching programs -Short Story Writing SeminarsTM^ creative writing program for 
5th through 8th graders) and The Program in Occasional Writing.TM 

-Ed 

I enter the St. Anthony office complex through a door on Golden Gate Avenue. Already at 
1 1 : 1 5 the line of persons waiting for Thanksgiving dinner runs from the entrance to the Dining 
Room on Jones Street up to Golden Gate Avenue and west on Golden Gate as far as Saint Boniface 
Church. 

The lights are off in the anteroom and library where more than a half dozen volunteers are 
waiting to serve, but the big front windows give reflected sunlight from the street. To my right at a 
big oak reading table sits a black woman in her early fifties who is dressed in a pleasant blue and 
white check dress with a scarf at her neck. Across the table, reading Thomas Merton's Seeds of 
Contemplation, sits a well-dressed man whose face shows a carefully-trimmed black goatee and 
heavy hornrim glasses. He looks up as I take a seat, says, "There will be a wait." As we talk, he 
reveals that he is studying in Berkeley to be a priest. 

Finally a St. Anthony's employee tells us we can 
"go down" to the dining room. The phrase implies that 
we are descending into an unknown nether world. We get 
aprons and sanitary paper hats and go down a narrow, 
steeply-pitched flight of stairs. 

In the dining room, the seminarian from Berkeley 
and I are approached by a St. Anthony's employee who 
asks us to work in the dishwashing room. We follow him 
through the serving area lined elbow-to-elbow with 
volunteers and out the other end, where the poor stoop 
to lower their trays as a young girl holding a large can 
spoons sugar into their coffee. 

I begin bussing clean trays and silverware and 
dishes with my friend the seminarian. Right out of the 
sterilizer the dishes are so hot we have to stack them 
quickly so our fingers don't get burned and then wait for 
the stacks to cool before we can move them. 

The St. Anthony's employee who has brought us 
here is talking to me during one of the waits. 

"Did you ever see poverty like this?" he asks. In 
the dining area every table is filled and the noise level 
little by little is increasing. And people are standing with 
their trays, looking for empty seats.
